title: Cline CLI npm Package Compromised via Suspected Cache Poisoning Attack

reading.body:
An AI system used for automated issue triage was deployed with broad permissions and no human approval step between its decisions and their execution. The system was vulnerable to prompt injection, a well-known failure mode where an attacker embeds instructions in a text input that the model treats as part of its legitimate task. By creating a GitHub issue with hidden malicious commands, an attacker could trick the AI into running arbitrary code with access to publishing credentials and cached build artifacts.

The vulnerability allowed an attacker to compromise the software supply chain by poisoning package repositories. The system had access to credentials for npm, the VS Code Marketplace, and OpenVSX, meaning a successful attack could distribute malicious code to millions of developers. What would have caught this is either removing the AI's ability to execute code without human review, filtering prompts for injection patterns, or restricting the permissions granted to the workflow to the minimum necessary for legitimate use.

It is not established whether the vulnerability was exploited to publish malicious packages or steal credentials, though the researcher noted that someone may have attempted an exploit. The team did not respond to responsible disclosure attempts and only fixed the issue after public disclosure.

summary:
# Summary

Cline, an open-source artificial intelligence coding tool used by millions of developers, had a critical security vulnerability from December 21, 2025 to February 9, 2026. The vulnerability existed in an automated issue triage workflow that used Claude AI and ran with broad permissions. An attacker could exploit a prompt injection flaw by creating a GitHub issue with malicious instructions. This would trick Claude into running arbitrary commands, allowing the attacker to poison GitHub Actions cache files and steal publishing credentials for the VS Code Marketplace, OpenVSX, and NPM repositories.

The researcher who discovered the vulnerability attempted to report it through official channels starting January 1, 2026, but received no response from the Cline team despite multiple contact attempts over more than a month. The researcher published the findings publicly on February 9, 2026, prompting Cline to fix the issue within an hour by removing the vulnerable workflow and rotating credentials. The researcher confirmed that while someone may have attempted to exploit the vulnerability, no malicious updates were released. Users are advised to disable auto-updates until Cline provides full details about potential unauthorized access.
